transcript:
This message comes from Angie. Angie has been helping homeowners find skilled pros
to get their home projects done well for over 30 years. For everything from minor repairs
to major remodels, find reviews, pricing, and booking at Angie.com or on the Angie app.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman. The state of Tennessee was not able
to put a condemned prisoner to death last night. Executioners gave inmate Krista Pike two separate
and lethal doses of the drug pentobarbital. She survived both attempts. Katherine Sweeney
is with member station WPLN. She was one of the media witnesses who saw the botched execution.
This is an enormous dose of a sedative. That should not ever need to happen twice, but it
did. And then she stayed alive. I think one of the issues we have here is the protocol doesn't
talk about what happens if you do this twice and they're still alive. I don't think that that is
something that was planned for. Katherine Sweeney reporting. Prison officials said later that they
moved Pike to a hospital for treatment. This is the second time this year that Tennessee
has botched an execution. President Trump has promised he would campaign to support Republicans
in 35 of the most competitive races. But NPR's Franco Ordonez reports he's kicking off a campaign
swing today in the more comfortably red state of Oklahoma. Starting in Oklahoma is a chance
to knock off some rust and workshop his campaign speech in front of a more friendly environment.
But it reminds Alex Conan, who worked in the George W. Bush White House of the 2006 midterms,
when Bush campaigned almost exclusively in red states. You can't go to a district or a state
where there's just as many Democrats as Republicans or where there's a lot of independent
voters because you're going to do more harm than good when your favorability numbers are this low.
That's because in a swing state, Trump is likely and perhaps more likely to stir up Democrats and
independent voters to go out and vote against Republicans. Franco Ordonez and PR News.
Starting today, states will be paying for a larger share of the bill to run the food
assistance program known as SNAP. NPR's Julianna Kim reports federal funding for costs,
including state SNAP workers, will shrink by half.
Last year's massive Republican tax and spending law, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act,
included major changes to how SNAP is funded, shifting more of the costs onto states rather
than the federal government. As a result, states may need to spend two to three times more in the
future in order to keep the food assistance program running. That's according to the Georgetown Center
on Poverty and Inequality. The key question now is how states will afford these new costs to SNAP.
Policy experts say states may need to raise taxes, cut funding for other programs,
or reduce access to food benefits. And it comes as SNAP participation is already rapidly dropping.
Julianna Kim, NPR News. You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Saudi Arabia is investigating yesterday's apparent attack on board a passenger plane
that landed at a Saudi airport. Passengers say the co-pilot attacked the pilot and then
tried to crash the plane. The co-pilot was subdued. Many passengers were Israeli and the
plane was headed for Tel Aviv. The Israeli government says this was terrorism.
An NPR investigation finds children with disabilities are the largest group in foster
care. NPR's Joe Shapiro reports they also have the worst outcomes in foster care.
NPR obtained data on a half million children and youth in foster care. Our analysis found that
disabled kids stay in foster care the longest, 50 percent longer than other children. They're
more likely to be moved from place to place and they're far more likely to live in institutional
settings rather than with a foster family. Another study found foster kids with physical
disabilities are nine times more likely to die. Nancy Thaler leads a federally funded program to
improve care for kids with tricky behavioral health issues. Kids who sometimes hurt themselves
or others. This is the group that everybody gives up on and it's because they have disabilities.
But Thaler says new brain science shows these kids can recover and lead successful lives.
Joseph Shapiro, NPR News. There are flood watches and warnings across much of the central U.S. today.
The remnants of a hurricane that hit Mexico are now streaming north. There are flash flood warnings
scattered across parts of Texas, Oklahoma and Iowa this morning. This is NPR.

President Trump kicks off campaign swing in Oklahoma rather than competitive districts
States begin paying larger share of SNAP food assistance program funding starting today
Saudi Arabia investigates apparent attack by co-pilot on passenger plane headed to Tel Aviv
NPR investigation finds children with disabilities are largest group in foster care with worst outcomes
Flood watches and warnings issued across central U.S. from remnants of Mexico hurricane
